areas_of_law: Federal public sector staffing / employment law
issues: Whether the employer abused its authority by adopting unpublished, undisclosed internal definitions and thresholds (12 months within 5 years) to interpret an ambiguous 'recent experience' qualification in a job poster

Whether classifying candidates' prior experience as qualifying or non-qualifying based on a chart pre-labelling job classifications (rather than assessing actual duties performed) constitutes an unreasonable or bad-faith application of the merit criteria

Whether characterizing pre-removal risk assessment officers as exercising quasi-judicial functions while treating front-line/inland enforcement officers' materially similar statutory decision-making (admissibility determinations, ministerial delegate authority) as purely administrative is an unreasonable or arbitrary distinction amounting to abuse of authority

Whether evidence that screening criteria were shaped to protect a class of employees facing upcoming position elimination supports an inference of improper purpose or bad faith in the design of the qualification standard

Whether the employer's refusal to reconsider after an informal discussion, including alleged inconsistent treatment of other candidates permitted to continue, gives rise to abuse of authority or a breach of the duty of fairness in the screening process

What standard of review a court or tribunal applies to a staffing/adjudicative body's acceptance of an employer's explanation for its screening criteria and its assessment of whether abuse of authority occurred

Whether the Public Service Employment Act's 'abuse of authority' standard permits an internal, unpublished definition of an ambiguous posted qualification, or whether fairness requires disclosure of such thresholds to applicants
key_facts: Complainant was a federal front-line immigration officer for approximately 12 years
He applied for an adjudicator position at a federal tribunal hearing protection claims
Poster required 'recent' experience in judicial/quasi-judicial decision-making, or research/inquiries in such settings, or in immigration, without specifying duration or recency threshold
Employer internally set an unpublished standard of 12 months' experience within the past 5 years
Screening committees used an internal reference guide and a chart pre-classifying job titles as qualifying or non-qualifying
The chart characterized pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA) officers as quasi-judicial decision-makers and front-line immigration officers as purely administrative
Only his 4 months in a PRRA-type role were credited; his 12 years of interviewing, admissibility determinations, criminal-equivalency analysis and database inquiries were not credited
Both officer types allegedly act as ministerial delegates under the same immigration statute
Case law reportedly holds PRRA officers are not a quasi-judicial body
Union-management minutes allegedly suggest the criteria were designed to protect PRRA officer positions facing elimination due to pending legislative reform
Complainant requested an informal discussion after being screened out and offered further detail on his duties, but employer declined to reconsider
Some other candidates were reportedly allowed to continue despite similar circumstances
causes_of_action: Complaint of abuse of authority in application of merit criteria under the Public Service Employment Act
Abuse of authority in choice of assessment method / screening process
Breach of procedural fairness in the informal discussion and reconsideration process
